# Kubernetes Infrastructure

# Kubernetes Infrastructure

Written by [Taki Sadik](../../about.html) · Last updated 2026-10-22 · 21 min read

Production-style 7-node Kubernetes cluster: Ubuntu Server VMs on bare-metal Proxmox hosts, one switch, one router, one wireless backhaul

## Overview

This project is a self-designed, self-built Kubernetes homelab: seven
        Ubuntu Server virtual machines running on bare-metal Proxmox VE hosts
        (3 desktop PCs and 4 laptops), interconnected through a single
        managed switch, a dedicated router handling inter-VLAN routing and NAT, and a wireless radio
        providing backhaul for the laptop nodes. The goal was to replicate a production-style
        container orchestration environment entirely from consumer hardware, with no cloud, no
        rented rack space, and no managed services.

The cluster runs kubeadm-bootstrapped Kubernetes on Ubuntu Server VMs
        provisioned inside Proxmox, with Calico as the CNI for pod networking and
        network policy enforcement, MetalLB for LoadBalancer services without a cloud provider,
        Longhorn for distributed persistent storage across nodes, and a full
        observability stack built on Prometheus + Grafana + Loki. Deployments are
        automated through Bash scripts, with application manifests versioned in Git; full GitOps
        with ArgoCD is a planned next step.

Every component, from the physical cable runs and VLAN trunking to the Kubernetes
        RBAC policies and Grafana dashboards, was planned, configured, and documented by hand.
        The cluster provides DNS, ingress, and monitoring for the homelab, and hosts the
        observability stack plus selected services in production. Note that the control plane is a
        single node, so this is a production-style homelab rather than a highly available
        production cluster: there is no API endpoint redundancy.

## Physical Topology

The entire infrastructure runs from a single physical location. Three desktop PCs serve as the
        primary compute and storage nodes, while four laptops act as lightweight worker nodes and
        provide redundancy. All wired nodes connect to a managed switch with 802.1Q VLAN trunking.
        The router handles inter-VLAN routing, DHCP reservation, and NAT to the public
        internet. Externally-facing services are published through Cloudflare Tunnel rather than
        inbound port forwards, so no ports are opened on the router (see the zero-trust build for
        the access design). A wireless radio bridges the laptop nodes
        into the cluster network over a dedicated 5 GHz backhaul link.

## Virtualization and Cluster Topology

No Kubernetes node runs directly on the hardware. Each physical machine is a
        Proxmox VE 8.x host, and every Kubernetes node is an Ubuntu Server
        24.04 virtual machine: 1 control plane plus 6 workers, for 7 nodes total. Each VM
        carries two virtual NICs, one on VLAN 20 (cluster traffic) and one on VLAN 30 (storage
        traffic). The diagram below shows the full stack, from bare-metal hosts to the nine
        hosted services.

## Network Architecture

Network segmentation is enforced at the switch level using three VLANs. The router performs
        inter-VLAN routing with firewall rules restricting lateral movement between segments. This
        mirrors enterprise network design where management, application, and storage traffic are
        isolated to prevent blast radius expansion during a compromise.

| VLAN | ID | Subnet | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Management | 10 | 10.10.10.0/24 | SSH access, Proxmox UI, router admin, switch management, IPMI/BMC |
| Cluster | 20 | 10.20.20.0/24 | Kubernetes API server, pod-to-pod (Calico with BGP peering between nodes on the same VLAN), MetalLB external IPs |
| Storage | 30 | 10.30.30.0/24 | NFS mounts, ZFS snapshot sync, backup traffic; Longhorn replica I/O only with the Longhorn storage network feature configured |

## Kubernetes Architecture

## Tech Stack

| Layer | Technology | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware | 3 × Desktop PC, 4 × Laptop | Physical hosts running Proxmox VE; the 7 K8s nodes are Ubuntu Server VMs on these hosts |
| Networking | Managed Switch (802.1Q), Router, 5 GHz Radio | VLAN segmentation, NAT, wireless mesh backhaul |
| Hypervisor | Proxmox VE 8.x | VM provisioning, snapshots, live migration |
| OS | Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS | Minimal server images inside Proxmox VMs |
| Container Runtime | containerd | CRI-compliant runtime for Kubernetes |
| Orchestration | Kubernetes (kubeadm) | Cluster bootstrapping, upgrades, node management |
| CNI | Calico | Pod networking, BGP peering, NetworkPolicy enforcement |
| Load Balancer | MetalLB (L2 mode) | External IP allocation for LoadBalancer services without a cloud provider |
| Ingress | Nginx Ingress Controller | HTTP/HTTPS routing, TLS termination, path-based routing |
| Storage | Longhorn | Distributed block storage with 3x replication across nodes |
| TLS | Let’s Encrypt + cert-manager | Automated certificate provisioning and renewal |
| Monitoring | Prometheus + Node Exporter | Metrics collection from nodes, pods, and Kubernetes internals |
| Dashboards | Grafana | Visualization, alerting rules, and SLA tracking |
| Logging | Loki + Promtail | Centralized log aggregation and querying |
| Automation | Bash, Docker Compose | Cluster provisioning scripts, auxiliary service orchestration |
| DNS | Pi-hole + Unbound | Internal cluster DNS resolution and ad/threat blocking |

## Build Process

### Hardware Preparation & Network Wiring

Each desktop PC and laptop was prepared with a clean BIOS/UEFI configuration, boot order
              set to PXE/USB, and hardware diagnostics run to verify RAM, disk health, and thermal
              performance. Cat6 Ethernet cables were run from each desktop to the managed switch.
              The switch was configured with three VLANs (10, 20, 30) and trunk ports for the router
              uplink. The wireless radio was mounted and configured in bridge mode on VLAN 20 to
              extend the cluster network to the laptop nodes over 5 GHz.

# Switch VLAN configuration (CLI example)
enable
configure terminal

vlan 10
  name MANAGEMENT
vlan 20
  name CLUSTER
vlan 30
  name STORAGE

# Trunk port to router
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
  switchport mode trunk
  switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30

# Access ports for desktop nodes (VLAN 20)
interface range GigabitEthernet0/2 - 4
  switchport mode access
  switchport access vlan 20

# Trunk port to wireless radio
interface GigabitEthernet0/5
  switchport mode trunk
  switchport trunk allowed vlan 20

### Proxmox Installation & VM Provisioning

Proxmox VE 8.x was installed on each of the seven hosts (3 desktops and
              4 laptops) as the base hypervisor. Ubuntu Server
              24.04 LTS VMs were created on each node with resource allocations matched to the
              hardware. VMs were configured with two virtual NICs: one on VLAN 20 (cluster traffic)
              and one on VLAN 30 (storage traffic). Cloud-init templates were used to standardize
              hostname, SSH keys, and network configuration across all VMs.

# Create a cloud-init template VM on Proxmox
qm create 9000 --name ubuntu-cloud --memory 4096 --cores 2 \
  --net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0,tag=20 \
  --net1 virtio,bridge=vmbr0,tag=30 \
  --scsihw virtio-scsi-single

# Import Ubuntu cloud image
qm set 9000 --scsi0 local-lvm:0,import-from=/var/lib/vz/template/iso/ubuntu-24.04-server-cloudimg-amd64.img
qm set 9000 --ide2 local-lvm:cloudinit
qm set 9000 --boot order=scsi0
qm set 9000 --serial0 socket --vga serial0

# Configure cloud-init defaults
qm set 9000 --ciuser taki --cipassword changeme \
  --sshkeys ~/.ssh/authorized_keys \
  --ipconfig0 ip=dhcp \
  --ipconfig1 ip=10.30.30.X/24,gw=10.30.30.1

# Clone template for each node (1 control plane + 6 workers)
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7; do
  qm clone 9000 10${i} --name k8s-node-${i} --full
  qm start 10${i}
done

### Kubernetes Cluster Bootstrap with kubeadm

All nodes were prepared with the Kubernetes prerequisites: swap disabled, kernel modules
              loaded (br_netfilter, overlay), sysctl parameters set for
              IP forwarding, and containerd installed as the CRI runtime. The control plane was
              initialized on PC-01, and worker nodes joined using the bootstrap token.

# Run on ALL nodes
cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/modules-load.d/k8s.conf
overlay
br_netfilter
EOF
sudo modprobe overlay && sudo modprobe br_netfilter

cat <<EOF | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/k8s.conf
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables  = 1
net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-ip6tables = 1
net.ipv4.ip_forward                 = 1
EOF
sudo sysctl --system

sudo swapoff -a && sudo sed -i '/swap/d' /etc/fstab

# Install containerd
sudo apt install -y containerd
sudo mkdir -p /etc/containerd
containerd config default | sudo tee /etc/containerd/config.toml
sudo sed -i 's/SystemdCgroup = false/SystemdCgroup = true/' /etc/containerd/config.toml
sudo systemctl restart containerd

# Install kubeadm, kubelet, kubectl
sudo apt install -y apt-transport-https ca-certificates curl gpg
curl -fsSL https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.30/deb/Release.key | \
  sudo gpg -dearmor -o /etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg
echo 'deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/kubernetes-apt-keyring.gpg] https://pkgs.k8s.io/core:/stable:/v1.30/deb/ /' | \
  sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list
sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y kubelet kubeadm kubectl
sudo apt-mark hold kubelet kubeadm kubectl

# Initialize control plane (PC-01)
sudo kubeadm init \
  --pod-network-cidr=192.168.0.0/16 \
  --apiserver-advertise-address=10.20.20.10 \
  --control-plane-endpoint=10.20.20.10:6443

mkdir -p $HOME/.kube
sudo cp /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf $HOME/.kube/config
sudo chown $(id -u):$(id -g) $HOME/.kube/config

# Join workers (run on each worker node)
sudo kubeadm join 10.20.20.10:6443 \
  --token <token> \
  --discovery-token-ca-cert-hash sha256:<hash>

### Calico CNI & Network Policy Deployment

Calico was deployed as the CNI plugin for pod networking with BGP peering between nodes
              and NetworkPolicy enforcement for micro-segmentation. Network policies were written to
              restrict pod-to-pod traffic: only explicitly allowed communication paths are permitted,
              following a default-deny ingress posture.

# Install Calico operator and custom resources
kubectl create -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/tigera-operator.yaml
kubectl create -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/projectcalico/calico/v3.28.0/manifests/custom-resources.yaml

# Verify Calico pods are running
kubectl get pods -n calico-system -w

# Default-deny ingress NetworkPolicy (applied per namespace)
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny-ingress
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
    - Ingress

# Allow only Nginx Ingress to reach web pods
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-ingress-to-web
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-nginx
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 80
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 443

### MetalLB & Nginx Ingress Controller

MetalLB was deployed in L2 (ARP) mode to provide external IP addresses for LoadBalancer
              services on the self-hosted cluster. An IP pool of 10.20.20.200–250 was
              reserved on VLAN 20. The Nginx Ingress Controller was deployed from the upstream
              bare-metal manifest to handle all HTTP/HTTPS traffic with TLS termination via
              cert-manager and Let’s Encrypt, and its Service is patched to type
              LoadBalancer so it is exposed through MetalLB.
              The pool must sit outside the router’s DHCP scope to avoid address conflicts.
              In L2 mode a single node answers ARP for each service IP, so failover between nodes
              takes a few seconds while ARP converges; that is acceptable for a homelab but it is
              not true active-active load balancing.

# Install MetalLB
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/metallb/metallb/v0.14.5/config/manifests/metallb-native.yaml

# Configure IP address pool
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: IPAddressPool
metadata:
  name: cluster-pool
  namespace: metallb-system
spec:
  addresses:
    - 10.20.20.200-10.20.20.250

---
apiVersion: metallb.io/v1beta1
kind: L2Advertisement
metadata:
  name: cluster-l2
  namespace: metallb-system

# Install Nginx Ingress Controller
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/ingress-nginx/controller-v1.10.1/deploy/static/provider/baremetal/deploy.yaml

# The bare-metal manifest ships the controller Service as NodePort;
# switch it to LoadBalancer so MetalLB assigns it an external IP
kubectl -n ingress-nginx patch svc ingress-nginx-controller \
  -p '{"spec":{"type":"LoadBalancer"}}'

# Install cert-manager for automated TLS
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/cert-manager/cert-manager/releases/download/v1.15.0/cert-manager.yaml

# ClusterIssuer for Let's Encrypt
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: taki@tyfsadik.org
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            class: nginx

### Longhorn Distributed Storage

Longhorn was deployed for persistent storage with 3x replication across the desktop
              nodes. Each desktop contributes its SSD/NVMe storage to the Longhorn pool. NFS, backup,
              and snapshot-sync traffic is isolated on VLAN 30 to prevent it from contending with
              cluster API and pod traffic on VLAN 20. Longhorn replica traffic uses the pod network
              by default; moving it to VLAN 30 requires configuring Longhorn’s storage network
              feature (Multus), which is a planned follow-up. Scheduled snapshots and backups to an
              NFS target provide recovery points.

# Install Longhorn
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/longhorn/longhorn/v1.6.2/deploy/longhorn.yaml

# Set as default StorageClass
kubectl patch storageclass longhorn -p \
  '{"metadata": {"annotations":{"storageclass.kubernetes.io/is-default-class":"true"}}}'

# Verify volumes and nodes
kubectl -n longhorn-system get pods
kubectl -n longhorn-system get nodes.longhorn.io

# Example PVC using Longhorn
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: nextcloud-data
  namespace: production
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  storageClassName: longhorn
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 100Gi

### Observability Stack: Prometheus + Grafana + Loki

The full observability stack was deployed using the kube-prometheus-stack Helm chart.
              Prometheus scrapes metrics from Node Exporter (hardware), kubelet (pod resources),
              kube-state-metrics (Kubernetes object states), and application-level exporters.
              Grafana provides pre-built dashboards for cluster health, node resources, pod
              performance, and Longhorn storage utilization. Loki with Promtail aggregates logs
              from all pods and system journals into a queryable interface within Grafana.

# Install Helm
curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/helm/helm/main/scripts/get-helm-3 | bash

# Add repos
helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo add grafana https://grafana.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update

# Install kube-prometheus-stack
helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack \
  --namespace monitoring --create-namespace \
  --set grafana.adminPassword='secureDashboard' \
  --set prometheus.prometheusSpec.retention=30d \
  --set prometheus.prometheusSpec.storageSpec.volumeClaimTemplate.spec.storageClassName=longhorn \
  --set prometheus.prometheusSpec.storageSpec.volumeClaimTemplate.spec.resources.requests.storage=50Gi

# Install Loki + Promtail
helm install loki grafana/loki-stack \
  --namespace monitoring \
  --set promtail.enabled=true \
  --set loki.persistence.enabled=true \
  --set loki.persistence.storageClassName=longhorn \
  --set loki.persistence.size=20Gi

# Expose Grafana via Ingress
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: grafana
  namespace: monitoring
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [grafana.tyfsadik.org]
      secretName: grafana-tls
  rules:
    - host: grafana.tyfsadik.org
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: monitoring-grafana
                port:
                  number: 80

## Services in the Homelab

Nine services run across the homelab. The cluster provides DNS, ingress, and the
        observability stack; the application services themselves are deployed a mix of ways,
        some as cluster workloads and some as Docker Compose or systemd deployments on
        dedicated hosts. Each service has its own project page with the exact deployment
        detail. The table below lists the service, the stack behind it, its namespace or host
        placement, domain, and purpose.

| Service | Stack | Placement | Domain | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nextcloud (cloud storage) | Nextcloud + MariaDB | Docker Compose on dedicated host | cloud.tyfsadik.org | Private file sync and sharing across devices, replacing hosted cloud drives |
| TYF-AI (private AI) | llama.cpp + Open WebUI | GPU host (see TYF-AI page) | ai.tyfsadik.org | Self-hosted LLM inference with integrated web search; model inference stays local |
| Pi-hole + Unbound DNS | Pi-hole + Unbound | Docker on network host | Internal | Network-wide DNS with ad and threat blocking plus recursive resolution |
| Email Server | Postfix + Dovecot, DKIM | Dedicated mail host | tyfsadik.org | Self-hosted SMTP/IMAP mail on the tyfsadik.org domain |
| SearXNG (search engine) | SearXNG + Nginx | Docker Compose on dedicated host | search.tyfsadik.org | Privacy-respecting metasearch aggregating results without tracking |
| Immich (photo server) | Immich + PostgreSQL | Docker Compose on media host | photo.tyfsadik.org | Photo and video backup with mobile auto-backup and ML face recognition |
| Kiwix (wiki mirror) | kiwix-serve + ZIM archives | systemd/Docker on wiki host | wiki.tyfsadik.org | Searchable offline Wikipedia mirror served from local ZIM files |
| Grafana Dashboards | Grafana (kube-prometheus-stack) | Cluster namespace: monitoring | grafana.tyfsadik.org | Cluster dashboards, alerting rules, and SLA tracking |
| Prometheus + Loki | Prometheus + Loki + Promtail | Cluster namespace: monitoring | Internal | Metrics collection and centralized log aggregation from all nodes and pods |

## Deployment Workflow

## Challenges & Solutions

- Laptop nodes dropping from cluster over Wi-Fi: The laptop worker nodes
          periodically lost connectivity over the wireless bridge, causing kubelet to miss heartbeats
          and the control plane to mark them as NotReady. Resolved by deploying a
          dedicated 5 GHz radio in bridge mode with a fixed channel, disabling power management on
          the laptop NICs (iw dev wlan0 set power_save off), and increasing the
          node-monitor-grace-period to 60s to tolerate brief interruptions without
          evicting pods.

- Longhorn replication saturating the network: Initial deployment placed
          backup, NFS, and snapshot-sync traffic on the same VLAN as cluster traffic, causing API
          server latency spikes during large write operations. Resolved by creating a dedicated
          VLAN 30 for that storage traffic. Note that Longhorn replica I/O itself rides the pod
          network by default; pinning it to VLAN 30 requires the Longhorn storage network feature
          (a Multus-backed secondary network), which is a planned follow-up rather than a
          completed step.

- MetalLB ARP conflicts with router DHCP: MetalLB’s L2 mode ARP
          responses conflicted with the router’s DHCP leases when the IP pool overlapped with
          the DHCP range. Fixed by reserving 10.20.20.200–250 as a static range
          excluded from DHCP and configuring MetalLB to only advertise within that range.

- etcd performance on a single control plane node: With only one control
          plane node, etcd write latency spiked during heavy scheduling. Mitigated by placing etcd
          data on the NVMe drive (not SSD), tuning heartbeat-interval and
          election-timeout, and ensuring no other I/O-heavy workloads run on PC-01.

- TLS certificate provisioning for multiple subdomains: cert-manager’s
          HTTP-01 solver required each subdomain to be publicly reachable, which conflicted with
          internal-only services. Resolved by using DNS-01 challenge validation for internal services
          and HTTP-01 for public-facing ones. DNS-01 needs a solver entry for the DNS provider
          (for example a Cloudflare API token solver), while the HTTP-01 ClusterIssuer shown in
          step 5 above covers the public subdomains.

- Resource contention on 8 GB laptop nodes: Laptops with only 8 GB RAM
          struggled when Longhorn and Prometheus exporters consumed too much memory alongside
          application pods. Fixed by applying resource limits and requests to all pods, tainting the
          laptop nodes with node-role=lightweight:PreferNoSchedule, and using node
          affinity rules to keep heavy workloads on the desktop nodes.

## Security Hardening

- RBAC: Least-privilege service accounts per namespace; no pods run with cluster-admin

- NetworkPolicy: Default-deny ingress on all namespaces; explicit allow rules per service

- Pod Security Standards: restricted profile enforced on application namespaces; infrastructure components that require it (Longhorn, CNI, ingress) run under the privileged standard with explicit exemptions, since they need host mounts and elevated capabilities

- Image Scanning: Trivy scans on all container images before deployment; CVE alerts sent to Grafana

- Secrets Management: Kubernetes Secrets encrypted at rest with aescbc encryption provider

- SSH Hardening: Key-only authentication, fail2ban on all nodes, management access restricted to VLAN 10

- Firewall Rules: Router ACLs restrict inter-VLAN traffic; only necessary ports open between segments

## What I Learned

- End-to-end Kubernetes cluster lifecycle: bootstrapping, upgrading, scaling, and troubleshooting with kubeadm

- On-premises networking for Kubernetes: VLAN segmentation, BGP with Calico, ARP-based load balancing with MetalLB

- Distributed storage engineering: Longhorn replication, IOPS tuning, and failure recovery across physical nodes

- Enterprise-grade observability: Prometheus metric design, Grafana alerting pipelines, Loki log correlation

- Physical infrastructure design: cable management, switch VLAN configuration, wireless backhaul for cluster nodes

- Security-first architecture: network micro-segmentation, RBAC design, pod security standards, image vulnerability scanning

- Resource management on heterogeneous hardware: taints, tolerations, affinity rules, and resource quotas to balance workloads across nodes with different capabilities

- The discipline of documentation: every configuration change logged, every decision recorded, every diagram kept current

## How I built it

This cluster exists to answer one question: how close to production-grade can you get with consumer hardware and zero cloud spend? The answer turned out to be a full stack, from VLAN-segmented networking up through GitOps-style deployments, running on three desktop PCs and four laptops.

- Phase 1, hardware and network prep: Rack-mounted three desktop PCs and four laptops, ran Cat6 to a managed switch, carved out VLANs 10 (management), 20 (cluster), and 30 (storage), and bridged the laptops in over a dedicated 5 GHz radio link.

- Phase 2, virtualization layer: Installed Proxmox VE 8.x on every host, then created seven Ubuntu Server 24.04 VMs with dual virtual NICs on the cluster and storage VLANs.

- Phase 3, bootstrap Kubernetes: Initialized the cluster with kubeadm: one control plane plus six workers, with etcd on the control plane.

- Phase 4, networking and storage: Deployed Calico for pod networking with NetworkPolicy, MetalLB in L2 mode for external IPs, the Nginx Ingress Controller for TLS termination, and Longhorn with 3x replication for block storage.

- Phase 5, observability and hardening: Added Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, and node exporters, then hardened with RBAC least privilege, default-deny NetworkPolicies, restricted pod security standards, Trivy image scanning, and secrets encrypted at rest.

- Phase 6, production workloads: Deployed the nine homelab services through a GitHub Actions CI pipeline with rolling updates.

## What you need

| Category | Item | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware | 3 desktop PCs and 4 laptops (or any 7 machines) | Mix of wired and wireless nodes works; wired is preferred for storage traffic |
| Hardware | Managed switch with 802.1Q VLAN support | Needed for the management, cluster, and storage segmentation |
| Hardware | Router handling NAT, DHCP, and inter-VLAN routing | Plus a 5 GHz radio if you want wireless worker nodes |
| Software | Proxmox VE 8.x, Ubuntu Server 24.04, kubeadm, containerd | The virtualization and orchestration base |
| Software | Calico, MetalLB, Nginx Ingress, Longhorn, Prometheus stack | Networking, storage, and observability |
| Skills | Linux networking, VLANs, and Kubernetes fundamentals | Troubleshooting spans all three layers |

## Challenges and lessons learned

- Wireless worker nodes: laptop nodes on the 5 GHz backhaul occasionally flap, which Kubernetes reads as node pressure. Lesson: tune node status timeouts for the reality of your network, and keep etcd off the wireless path.

- Longhorn over mixed links: 3x replication assumes healthy replica paths; a slow wireless replica drags write latency. Lesson: place replicas with topology awareness so the fast wired nodes carry the quorum.

- Laptop power management: laptops love to sleep, and a sleeping kubelet looks like a dead node. Lesson: disable every sleep and lid behavior in the OS and BIOS before joining the cluster.

## What is next

- Evaluate Talos Linux for immutable, API-driven node management.

- Move deployments to full GitOps with ArgoCD and sealed secrets.

- Add external-dns and cert-manager automation for hands-free service onboarding.

- Experiment with IPv6 on the cluster VLAN for dual-stack experience.

## Related Work

- Proxmox Homelab, a separate single-host Proxmox build; the 7-node cluster runs on Proxmox VE installed on its own 3 desktops and 4 laptops.

- Proxmox Zero-Trust Private Cloud, identity-aware access in front of cluster services.

- Data Sovereignty Stack, storage and backup for stateful cluster workloads.

# Proxmox VE Homelab: Zero-Trust Private Cloud

# Proxmox VE Homelab: Zero-Trust Private Cloud

Written by [Taki Sadik](../../about.html) · Last updated 2026-10-22 · 15 min read

A 3-node Proxmox VE HA cluster with Ceph storage, VLAN segmentation, and zero-trust external access via Cloudflare Tunnel with Tailscale mesh fallback.

## Overview

This private cloud keeps every self-hosted service reachable with zero open inbound ports. A 3-node Proxmox VE 8.1 cluster provides high availability over Ceph; the network is segmented into four VLANs by trust level; and the only path in from the internet is a Cloudflare Tunnel gated by Access policies, with Tailscale as an authenticated mesh fallback. No inbound ports are open on the homelab router, and tunnel traffic rides Cloudflare's edge network for low-latency global access.

This is a distinct build from the single-host Proxmox Homelab and from the 7-node Kubernetes cluster's own Proxmox underlay: these three nodes are dedicated to this HA cluster, and it is this cluster's services that the Cloudflare Tunnel publishes.

On three nodes, Ceph runs its monitors in quorum with pools at 3x replication, so any single node can fail without data loss, but there is no second failure margin and recovery is I/O heavy on consumer disks. Placement group counts were therefore tuned down from the Ceph defaults, trading slower recovery for stability, and Proxmox HA is set so guests restart on a surviving node when one fails.

## Network Topology

## Zero-Trust Access Flow

## Implementation

### Form the HA cluster

### Expose a service via Cloudflare Tunnel (no open ports)

### Automate local ZFS snapshots with sanoid

Sanoid protects the nodes' local ZFS pools (rpool). Ceph volumes are a separate scope: they need their own snapshot or backup strategy (Ceph snapshots, rbd mirroring, or vzdump to external storage), since sanoid does not see Ceph RBD images.

rpool/data@autosnap_2026-06-17_00:00:00_daily   ... 30 kept
took 12 snapshots, pruned 3

## Key Results

- Removed all open inbound ports by routing every external path through Cloudflare Tunnel gated by Access policies.

- Low-latency global access via Cloudflare's edge network, with Tailscale as an authenticated mesh fallback.

- Automated local ZFS snapshots (hourly/daily) with 30-day retention via sanoid; Ceph volumes are covered by a separate snapshot strategy.

- Proxmox HA configured across the 3 nodes so guests restart on a surviving node if one fails.

## Related Work

- Proxmox Homelab (foundation build)

- Data Sovereignty & Secure Media Stack

- VLAN Configuration Lab

## How I built it

The design brief was strict: every self-hosted service reachable from anywhere, with zero public ingress. That means no open ports at all, identity-checked access at the edge, and a fallback path that stays authenticated.

- Phase 1, form the HA cluster: Joined three Proxmox VE 8.1 nodes with pvecm and built Ceph shared storage across them for high availability.

- Phase 2, segment the network: Carved the network into four VLANs by trust level: 10 for management, 20 for production, 30 for IoT, and 40 as the DMZ.

- Phase 3, close every port: Exposed services exclusively through Cloudflare Tunnel with Access policies, so the only path in from the internet is identity-gated and no inbound ports are open on the homelab router.

- Phase 4, add the mesh fallback: Configured Tailscale as an authenticated fallback so admin access survives even if the tunnel path has issues.

- Phase 5, automate data protection: Set up sanoid for automated local ZFS snapshots with hourly, daily, and 30-day retention, plus a separate snapshot strategy for Ceph volumes.

- Phase 6, deploy services: Ran the Docker-based services in LXC containers on the production VLAN behind the zero-trust front door.

## What you need

| Category | Item | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware | 3 Proxmox nodes with redundant networking | Quorum needs three; Ceph wants separate fast links |
| Software | Proxmox VE 8.1, Ceph, sanoid | Clustering, distributed storage, snapshot automation |
| Software | cloudflared, Cloudflare Access | Tunnel ingress with identity policies |
| Software | Tailscale | Authenticated mesh fallback |
| Accounts | Cloudflare account with a domain | Tunnel DNS routing and Access policies |
| Skills | VLAN design and Ceph fundamentals | Placement groups, crush maps, and recovery behavior |

## Challenges and lessons learned

- Ceph on three small nodes: Ceph assumes datacenter hardware and complains loudly on consumer gear. Lesson: tune placement group counts down and accept slower recovery in exchange for stability.

- Quorum sensitivity: losing one node in a three-node cluster leaves no failure margin. Lesson: monitor quorum health as a first-class alert, not an afterthought.

- Access policy UX: every new service needs its Access policy or users hit a wall. Lesson: template the policy creation alongside the tunnel route so nothing ships ungated.

## What is next

- Enforce device posture checks through WARP before granting access.

- Move toward short-lived certificates for service-to-service auth.

- Build an audit logging pipeline for every access decision.

- Expand automated policy tests that verify each VLAN boundary.

## Requirements & Engineering Objectives

The build was scoped before any hardware was racked. The driving requirement was a hard
        one: every self-hosted service reachable from anywhere, with zero public ingress. Each
        objective below maps to a design element documented on this page.

| Objective | Category | Design Target | Where Addressed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Services reachable from anywhere | Functional | Public hostnames served without any inbound port forward on the router | Cloudflare Tunnel (Implementation step 2) |
| No open inbound ports | Security | Router exposes zero listeners to the internet; all ingress is egress-originated | Security Design |
| Identity checked at the edge | Security | A Cloudflare Access policy gates every public hostname before traffic reaches a service | Zero-Trust Access Flow |
| Admin access survives tunnel failure | Reliability | An authenticated fallback path independent of Cloudflare | Tailscale mesh fallback |
| Tolerate a single node failure | Reliability | Ceph pools at 3x replication across 3 nodes; Proxmox HA restarts guests on a survivor | Architecture Deep-Dive |
| Point-in-time recovery | Reliability | Automated hourly/daily ZFS snapshots with 30-day retention on local pools | sanoid (Implementation step 3) |
| Contain lateral movement | Security | Four VLANs segmented by trust level with router-side firewalling between segments | Network Topology |

Constraints were stated up front and accepted, not worked around silently: exactly three
        nodes (quorum arithmetic leaves no second failure margin), consumer-grade disks (Ceph
        recovery is I/O heavy, so placement group counts were tuned down), a residential ISP
        uplink, and a homelab budget that rules out rented rack space or duplicate WAN links.

## Architecture Deep-Dive

Two flows define the system. The first is the ingress path: a request reaches the
        Cloudflare edge, passes the Access identity and policy check, and rides the tunnel that
        cloudflared established outbound from the DMZ VLAN. Because the tunnel is
        initiated from inside, no inbound port is ever opened. The second path is the fallback:
        Tailscale forms an authenticated WireGuard mesh that reaches the management VLAN
        directly, bypassing Cloudflare entirely.

Storage follows the same three-node symmetry. Every Ceph pool is configured at 3x
        replication: a guest write lands on a primary OSD and is replicated to an OSD on each of
        the other two nodes before it is acknowledged. Three monitors run one per node and hold
        quorum at 2-of-3, so the cluster keeps serving reads and writes with any one node down,
        and Proxmox HA restarts the failed node's guests on a surviving host.

## Component Reference

Status labels are honest about what this repository contains. This page is documentation,
        so items are marked Documented unless the page itself shows verification
        output; work that is described but not yet built is marked Planned.

| Component | Responsibility | Technology | Dependencies | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HA cluster membership | Node quorum, cluster configuration, guest restart on failure | Proxmox VE 8.1 (pvecm, corosync) | 3 nodes, management VLAN | Documented |
| Shared storage | Replicated block storage for guest disks across all nodes | Ceph (MON, MGR, OSD; 3x replication) | Proxmox cluster, tuned PG counts | Documented |
| Zero-ingress publishing | Outbound-only tunnel carrying public traffic to services | cloudflared | Cloudflare account, tunnel DNS routes | Documented |
| Identity gate | Per-hostname authentication and authorization before any request reaches a service | Cloudflare Access | Cloudflare Tunnel, identity provider | Documented |
| Fallback access | Authenticated admin path to the management VLAN independent of Cloudflare | Tailscale (WireGuard mesh) | Tailscale account, ACLs | Documented |
| Snapshot automation | Hourly/daily local ZFS snapshots with 30-day retention on rpool | sanoid | ZFS pools on each node | Verified (sampled output shown above) |
| Network segmentation | Four trust-level VLANs (10 mgmt, 20 prod, 30 IoT, 40 DMZ) with router firewalling | 802.1Q switch config, router ACLs | Managed switch, router | Documented |
| Service workloads | Docker-based services behind the tunnel | Docker inside LXC on VLAN 20 | Proxmox cluster, Ceph storage | Documented |
| Ceph data protection | Snapshot or backup strategy for RBD volumes (outside sanoid's scope) | Ceph snapshots, rbd mirroring, or vzdump | Ceph cluster, external storage target | Planned |
| Device posture checks | Require device health signals before Access grants a request | Cloudflare WARP | Cloudflare Access | Planned |
| Access audit pipeline | Log every access decision for review | To be selected | Cloudflare Access logs | Planned |
| Policy boundary tests | Automated checks that each VLAN boundary actually blocks what it should | To be selected | VLAN segmentation | Planned |

## Security Design

The design applies zero-trust principles at homelab scale: no implicit trust for any
        network location, identity verified on every external request, and blast radius limited
        by segmentation.

- Egress-only ingress model: cloudflared initiates the tunnel
          outbound to Cloudflare's edge. The homelab router forwards no inbound ports, so the
          entire public attack surface collapses to the Cloudflare edge, where Access policies
          authenticate and authorize before any byte reaches a service.

- Per-service policy, no blanket rules: each hostname published through
          the tunnel gets its own Access policy; a new service is not reachable until its policy
          exists. This is why policy creation is templated alongside the tunnel route, so nothing
          ships ungated.

- Authenticated fallback: Tailscale provides a second, independent path
          into the management VLAN. It is a WireGuard mesh with its own identity and ACLs, so a
          Cloudflare outage does not become an administrative lockout, and the fallback is never
          an unauthenticated backdoor.

- Segmentation by trust level: management (VLAN 10), production (VLAN 20),
          IoT (VLAN 30), and DMZ (VLAN 40) are isolated at the switch, with the router firewalling
          between segments. A compromised IoT device cannot reach the Proxmox management plane.

- Certificate and credential handling: TLS for public hostnames is
          terminated at the Cloudflare edge, so no certificate private keys need to live on the
          tunnel-published services. The tunnel credentials file and any API tokens are stored
          only on the host that runs cloudflared, with restrictive file permissions;
          commands on this page use placeholders such as <API_TOKEN> rather
          than real values.

- Planned hardening: device posture enforcement via WARP, short-lived
          certificates for service-to-service authentication, and an audit pipeline over every
          Access decision are designed but not yet implemented (see the component reference and
          limitations).

## Failure Modes & Recovery

Each failure mode below follows from the architecture described above. Commands are
        sanitized: real hostnames, tokens, and IDs are replaced with placeholders.

### Cloudflare outage or tunnel down

Public hostnames stop resolving to a working path, but nothing inside the cluster is
        affected. Administration continues over the Tailscale fallback, which never touches
        Cloudflare. Recovery on the DMZ host:

### Single node failure

Ceph monitors hold quorum at 2-of-3, so the surviving two nodes keep the cluster
        read-write. OSDs on the failed node go down; Ceph marks the pool degraded and begins
        re-replicating data onto the surviving OSDs. Proxmox HA restarts the failed node's guests
        on a surviving host. This is the case the design explicitly tolerates; recovery is I/O
        heavy on consumer disks, which is why PG counts were tuned down for stability over speed.

### Second node failure before the first recovers

With only one node left, corosync and the Ceph monitors lose quorum: the cluster goes
        read-only and guests stop rather than risk split-brain. This is the accepted limit of a
        three-node design. After hardware is repaired, rejoining the node lets Ceph backfill and
        rebalance automatically. If the failed node cannot return, quorum can be temporarily
        adjusted as a deliberate, documented break-glass step:

### ZFS snapshot rollback on a local pool

sanoid keeps hourly and daily snapshots for 30 days on each node's rpool. Rolling back
        discards everything written after the snapshot, so it is a deliberate operation:

### Ceph RBD data

sanoid does not see Ceph RBD images, so guest disks on Ceph need the separate strategy
        noted in the component reference (Ceph snapshots, rbd mirroring, or vzdump to external
        storage). Until that is built, a Ceph pool loss has no point-in-time recovery; this is
        listed as a limitation below.

## Troubleshooting Matrix

| Symptom | Possible Cause | Diagnostic | Safe Remediation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Public hostname returns 502/503 or times out | cloudflared not running, tunnel route missing, or origin service down | systemctl status cloudflared; cloudflared tunnel list; curl the service locally on VLAN 20 | Restart cloudflared; re-add the DNS route with cloudflared tunnel route dns <TUNNEL_NAME> <hostname>; restart the LXC service if the tunnel is healthy |
| Users hit an Access deny page on a new service | Hostname published without a matching Access policy | Check the Access application list for the hostname in the Cloudflare dashboard | Create the Access policy from the template used at tunnel-route time; never publish a route without its policy |
| ceph -s shows HEALTH_WARN, degraded PGs | Node or OSD down; re-replication in progress after a failure | ceph osd tree; ceph health detail; pvecm status | Let backfill finish if a node just returned; if an OSD is permanently gone, replace it and let Ceph rebalance; avoid restarts during recovery |
| Cluster commands hang; guests stopped unexpectedly | Quorum lost (two nodes down or corosync partition) | pvecm status on each reachable node; check management VLAN connectivity | Restore node connectivity first; use pvecm expected 1 only as a documented break-glass step while rebuilding |
| Snapshots missing or retention drifting | sanoid timer failed, pool full, or config error | systemctl status sanoid.timer; zfs list -t snapshot -r rpool; zpool list for capacity | Fix the config and restart the timer; free pool space above 80% usage; run sanoid once manually to confirm snapshots are taken and pruned |
| Tailscale fallback unreachable | Node's tailscaled down, ACL change, or expired node key | tailscale status and tailscale ping <node> from an admin device | Restart tailscaled on the node; re-authenticate the node key; review recent ACL changes before reverting anything |
| Guests do not restart after a node failure | HA resources not configured for the guest, or surviving node lacks capacity | Check the HA resource list in Proxmox; review the HA manager log on a surviving node | Add the guest as an HA resource; keep enough headroom on each node to absorb one node's guests |

## Limitations & Future Work

- No second failure margin: three nodes means quorum at 2-of-3 and Ceph at 3x replication. One failure is tolerated by design; a second concurrent failure stops the cluster. This is accepted, monitored, and documented rather than hidden.

- Consumer disks bound Ceph recovery: re-replication after a node loss is slow and I/O heavy. PG counts are tuned down for stability, which trades away recovery speed.

- Ceph RBD has no point-in-time recovery yet: sanoid covers only local ZFS pools. The separate snapshot or backup strategy for Ceph volumes (Ceph snapshots, rbd mirroring, or vzdump to external storage) is planned, not built.

- Cloudflare is a dependency: public access depends on the tunnel and Access. The Tailscale fallback covers administration, but it does not restore public service reachability during a Cloudflare outage.

- Single residential uplink: one ISP, one router. The zero-trust design removes the need for inbound ports, but it cannot remove the physical single point of failure.

- Posture, audit, and policy testing are unfinished: WARP device posture, an access-decision audit pipeline, short-lived service certificates, and automated VLAN boundary tests are the active next steps listed above.

## References

- Proxmox VE Cluster Manager (pvecm) documentation

- Proxmox VE High Availability documentation

- Proxmox VE hyper-converged Ceph cluster guide

- Ceph official documentation (replication, placement groups, monitors and quorum)

- Cloudflare Tunnel (cloudflared) documentation

- Cloudflare Access policies documentation

- Tailscale knowledge base (mesh networking and ACLs)

- OpenZFS documentation (snapshots and rollback)

- sanoid (ZFS snapshot automation and retention policy)

# Chakor: Your AI, on Your Hardware

# Chakor: Your AI, on Your Hardware

Written by [Taki Sadik](../../about.html) · Last updated 2026-10-22 · 18 min read

An open-source AI workspace you run yourself. Local and cloud models, web search, document chat, model compare, notes, and memory, all private on your own machine.

## What You Will Learn / Do

- Stand up a private AI workspace with Docker, a one-command installer, or a manual dev build.

- Connect local engines (llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio) or bring your own cloud API keys.

- Download GGUF models from Hugging Face in-app and switch models from the UI, no terminal.

- Stack: Next.js 15, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind, SQLite (better-sqlite3), Auth.js v5 · License: MIT

## Overview

Chakor is an open-source AI workspace that runs entirely on hardware you control. Point it at a local model or your own API keys, then chat, search the web, talk to your documents, compare models side by side, and run real research. Conversations live in a SQLite database on your disk, not in someone else's data center. It is a lighter, friendlier alternative to Open WebUI and an open-source answer to LM Studio that also runs on a server and on your phone.

Three things set it apart: it reads your RAM and GPU and tags every model FITS, TIGHT, or TOO BIG so you never load one that crashes; it downloads GGUF models from Hugging Face in the background straight into your models folder; and it switches between llama.cpp, Ollama, and LM Studio in one tap, freeing the previous model first so two never fight for the same VRAM.

## Architecture Overview

One file, no database server: better-sqlite3 keeps the whole workspace in a single SQLite file, which makes backup and migration trivial. The tradeoff is write serialization, so WAL mode and short transactions matter once multiple users write concurrently; read-heavy single-node use is where this design shines.

## Quick Start

Pick whichever fits you. All three end with the app on http://localhost:3001. The first account you register becomes the admin. The default registration mode is invite; the default invite code is change-me, so change INVITE_CODE in your .env before exposing the app. For a solo setup, you can set REGISTRATION_MODE=open instead.

### Option 1: Docker (Linux, macOS, Windows)

The least-fuss path. Install Docker, then clone and bring it up; a secret key is generated and stored in the data volume.

### Option 2: One-command installer (Linux, macOS, Android)

The hands-off path. The installer detects your OS and package manager and installs Git, a build chain, Node 20+, and Ollama, then starts Chakor. On Android, run the same command inside Termux and your phone becomes the server.

### Option 3: Manual (for developers)

## Get a Model

Chakor needs something to talk to. The simplest route is Ollama; Chakor auto-discovers its installed models.

- llama.cpp: point LLAMA_SERVER_BIN at your llama-server and Chakor supervises it. No model yet? Use Settings → Models → Download from Hugging Face, with a fit tag per quant.

- Cloud keys: set OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GOOGLE_AI_API_KEY, or one OPENROUTER_API_KEY for hundreds of models.

- Hardware-aware: Settings → Models shows detected RAM/GPU and marks each model FITS, TIGHT, or TOO BIG with a RECOMMENDED pick.

## How Model Switching Works

Switch model per message from the chat header, flip engines (llama.cpp / Ollama / LM Studio) in one tap, and download in the background so you can close the tab. On a roomy GPU, enable "keep multiple models loaded" for instant switching; on a modest machine it stays safely one-at-a-time so two models never OOM.

## Key Features

- Models, your way: local (Ollama/LM Studio/llama.cpp, GPU or CPU) and cloud (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter), switchable per message.

- Knowledge + web: built-in web search (SearXNG → Brave → DuckDuckGo fallback), document chat (PDF/text/markdown), and a cited research mode.

- More than a chat box: blind A/B Compare with a leaderboard, cross-conversation Memory, a Keep-style Notes panel, folders/tags/archive, vision input, and shareable links.

- Private + yours: no telemetry, local SQLite storage, multi-user with an admin panel, a live theme editor, and full rebrand from one config file. Installable as a PWA on phone and desktop.

## Testing & Validation

After startup, open http://localhost:3001 and register the first (admin) account, then confirm a model responds:

You should see 200, the model picker should list your Ollama/LM Studio models or cloud providers, and a test prompt should stream a reply. If all three hold, your private AI workspace is live.

**Q: Troubleshooting**

## Key Results

- Delivered a self-hosted AI workspace with local conversation storage and no telemetry. Note: enabling cloud providers or web search sends message content and derived queries outside your machine.

- Unified 3 local engines plus 4+ cloud providers behind one UI, switchable per message.

- Added hardware-aware model fit tagging that prevents out-of-memory crashes on load.

- Shipped a hands-off installer that provisions every dependency in one command.

## Related Work

- TYF-AI: Self-Hosted Local AI Security Platform

- Custom LLM from Scratch (Proposed Protocol)

- Proxmox Zero-Trust Private Cloud

## How I built it

Chakor started as my answer to a privacy problem: I wanted a modern AI workspace, but I did not want my prompts, documents, or notes leaving my own hardware. The design keeps every byte local by default while still supporting cloud models for the moments a local GPU is not enough.

- Phase 1, application skeleton: Built the Next.js and TypeScript frontend with server-side API routes, backed by SQLite so the whole app runs from a single file database with no external services.

- Phase 2, model backends: Integrated local runtimes (Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio) alongside optional cloud providers, with a unified interface so switching models never changes the workflow.

- Phase 3, knowledge features: Added document chat with retrieval, live web search, and a model comparison view so answers can be checked side by side.

- Phase 4, personal workspace: Added notes and long-term memory so the assistant builds context across sessions instead of starting cold every time.

- Phase 5, packaging and release: Containerized the stack with Docker and published it as open source under the MIT license so anyone can self-host it.

## What you need

| Category | Item | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware | Any modern PC; a GPU helps for larger local models | Small models run on CPU; 7B+ models benefit strongly from VRAM |
| Software | Node.js, Next.js, TypeScript, SQLite | The app stack, all open source |
| Software | Ollama, llama.cpp, or LM Studio | At least one local model runtime |
| Software | Docker and Docker Compose | For the one-command self-hosted deployment |
| Skills | JavaScript/TypeScript and basic LLM concepts | Prompting, context windows, model quantization basics |

## Challenges and lessons learned

- Model switching state: each backend has its own quirks for streaming and context limits, so a clean abstraction layer was needed. Lesson: hide provider differences behind one interface early, before the UI depends on any of them.

- Streaming reliability: server-sent event streams can drop on flaky networks, leaving half-rendered answers. Lesson: add client-side reconnection and treat every stream as resumable.

- Memory without bloat: storing everything forever makes retrieval noisy. Lesson: keep memory summaries compact and let the user inspect and delete what the assistant remembers.

## What is next

- Deeper document intelligence: multi-document comparison and cited answers with source highlighting.

- Voice input and output for hands-free sessions.

- A plugin system so community integrations do not require forking the codebase.

- Mobile-friendly UI refinements for the workspace on phones and tablets.

## Request Lifecycle

Every chat message travels the same path through the stack, from the browser down to a
        model engine and back. The flow below follows the modules named in the architecture
        diagram: the API route authenticates and validates the request, the dispatcher trims the
        conversation to fit the model’s context window and selects a provider, optional
        tools (web search and document retrieval) add grounding, the engine streams tokens back
        to the browser, and the finished exchange is persisted to the local SQLite database.

Two branches in this flow decide where your data goes, and the next section breaks them
        down: the local/cloud decision at inference time, and the tool decision that can send
        derived search queries to external search providers even when the model itself is local.

## Privacy Architecture

Chakor is private by default, not private unconditionally. The boundary depends on which
        engine and which tools a message uses, and the UI makes that boundary explicit rather
        than hiding it.

- Local inference keeps data on your hardware. When a message runs on
          llama.cpp, Ollama, or LM Studio, the prompt, conversation history, retrieved document
          chunks, and memory are processed on the host machine. The only routine network traffic
          in this mode is downloading GGUF models from Hugging Face, which sends no user content.

- Cloud providers receive what you send them. When a message is routed to
          OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or OpenRouter, the prompt and the assembled context (including
          memory and any retrieved document text) leave your machine and are processed under that
          provider’s data policy. This is a per-message choice, so sensitive chats can stay
          local while cloud models handle the rest.

- Web search leaves regardless of model. Enabling web search sends derived
          queries to SearXNG, Brave, or DuckDuckGo. A local model does not make search local; the
          query content is visible to whichever search backend answers it.

- Storage is a file you own. Conversations, notes, and memory live in one
          SQLite database on your disk. There is no telemetry and no sync to an external service;
          backup and deletion are ordinary file operations.

- Shared links are a deliberate exception. The shareable-link feature
          makes a chat readable by anyone who has the link, so treat sharing as publishing.

## Component Reference

The table below maps each component to its responsibility, technology, and dependencies.
        Status is reported honestly: Documented means the component is described in the
        project repository and documentation as shipped; it does not mean the implementation was
        independently audited for this page. Planned means it appears in the roadmap
        only.

| Component | Responsibility | Technology | Dependencies | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Web UI | Chat interface, model picker, settings, notes panel, compare view | Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind | App server API routes | Documented |
| Chat API | Authenticate session, validate input, stream responses (module /api/chat) | Next.js API routes, TypeScript | Auth.js session, dispatcher | Documented |
| System prompt | Baseline assistant behavior (lib/system-prompt.ts) | TypeScript | None | Documented |
| Dispatcher | Route messages to a provider, trim context to the model window (lib/dispatch.ts) | TypeScript | Provider layer | Documented |
| Provider layer | Unified interface over Ollama, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenRouter (lib/providers.ts) | TypeScript | Provider APIs, cloud API keys | Documented |
| llama.cpp supervisor | Spawn and manage the local llama-server child process, free models before switching (lib/llama-supervisor.ts) | TypeScript, llama.cpp | llama.cpp binary, GGUF models | Documented |
| Agent + tools | Function calling for tool use (lib/agent.ts, lib/tools.ts) | TypeScript | Search and retrieval modules | Documented |
| Web search | Live search with fallback chain SearXNG → Brave → DuckDuckGo (lib/searxng.ts) | TypeScript | SearXNG instance or search APIs | Documented |
| Document retrieval | Chunk and retrieve document context for chat (lib/rag.ts) | TypeScript | SQLite, uploaded documents | Documented |
| Database | Persist chats, messages, notes, memory, users (lib/db.ts) | SQLite via better-sqlite3 | Local filesystem | Documented |
| Authentication | Accounts, sessions, first-account admin, invite-gated registration | Auth.js v5 | SQLite, AUTH_SECRET | Documented |
| Model downloads | Background GGUF downloads from Hugging Face with hardware fit tags | TypeScript, Hugging Face hub | Network access, disk space | Documented |
| Installer | OS detection, dependency provisioning, optional systemd service | Bash (install.sh) | Git, Node 20+, package manager | Documented |
| Container deployment | One-command self-hosted run | Docker Compose | Docker, optional Ollama profile | Documented |
| Plugin system | Community integrations without forking | To be determined | Core API stabilization | Planned |
| Voice input/output | Hands-free sessions | To be determined | Browser speech APIs or local models | Planned |

## AI Security

Self-hosting moves the trust boundary onto your own machine, but an AI workspace still has
        its own attack surface: API keys, untrusted retrieved text, and expensive compute. The
        items below distinguish what the project documents from what remains a design goal.

- API key handling (documented pattern): cloud provider keys are set as
          server-side environment variables (OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY,
          GOOGLE_AI_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY), for example
          OPENAI_API_KEY=<your-openai-key> in .env.local or the
          Docker environment. Keys never ship to the browser. Design goal: encryption of
          stored secrets at rest and per-user keys are not currently documented, so treat the host
          environment file as the security boundary and restrict its file permissions accordingly.

- Input validation (documented): the chat API authenticates the session and
          validates input before dispatch, and the dispatcher trims conversations to the target
          model’s context window rather than letting unbounded history through.

- Prompt injection via tools (design goal): document chat and web search
          both inject third-party text into the model’s context, and that text can contain
          adversarial instructions (“ignore previous instructions”). The mitigation
          direction is to treat retrieved content as data, not commands: wrap search results and
          document chunks in clear delimiters, keep tool outputs visible to the user, and cite
          sources so injected claims are attributable. This is a stated design goal, not a
          verified control; assume a determined injection in a retrieved page can still influence
          answers.

- Resource exhaustion (partially documented): local inference is naturally
          bounded by the host, and the FITS / TIGHT / TOO BIG fit tagging prevents loading models
          that would exhaust memory, while the supervisor frees the previous model before switching
          so two never contend for the same VRAM. Design goal: per-user request rate
          limits and token budgets are not yet documented, so an authenticated user can still queue
          arbitrarily expensive requests; put the app behind a reverse proxy with request limits if
          you expose it to others.

- Registration control (documented): the default registration mode is
          invite-only with a default invite code of change-me; change
          INVITE_CODE before exposing the app, or set
          REGISTRATION_MODE=open only for a solo setup. The first registered account
          becomes the admin.

- Audit logging (design goal): an admin panel exists for multi-user
          management, but a structured audit log of logins, provider use, and admin actions is not
          documented. If you run Chakor for a team, front it with a reverse proxy that logs
          requests until first-party audit logging lands.

## Data Model

Persistence is deliberately simple: better-sqlite3 keeps the whole workspace in a single
        SQLite file with no database server. At the level this page documents, the store revolves
        around four entities — chats and their messages, plus the notes and memories that
        give the assistant continuity across sessions. The diagram below is an illustrative
        sketch of those relationships, not a verified schema dump; the authoritative schema lives
        in the repository.

The single-file design makes backup, migration, and full deletion trivial file operations.
        The tradeoff is write serialization: SQLite allows one writer at a time, so WAL mode and
        short transactions matter once multiple users write concurrently. For the read-heavy,
        single-node deployments Chakor targets, that tradeoff is the right one.

## Deployment

The Quick Start above covers the three install paths; this section is about running the
        result as a service you trust. A typical self-hosted deployment looks like this:

- Install: use Docker Compose (with the ollama profile if you
          want a bundled local engine) or the unattended installer
          (sudo bash install.sh --yes --service) which registers a systemd unit for
          24/7 operation.

- Configure secrets before first exposure: generate
          AUTH_SECRET with openssl rand -base64 32, replace the default
          INVITE_CODE=<your-invite-code>, and add any cloud keys you intend to
          use, for example ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<your-anthropic-key>. Keep the
          environment file readable only by the service account.

- Put HTTPS in front: Chakor serves HTTP on port 3001; terminate TLS at a
          reverse proxy (Nginx, Caddy, or a tunnel such as Cloudflare Tunnel, matching the rest of
          this homelab) before exposing it beyond localhost.

- Point it at models: pull an Ollama model, load one in LM Studio, set
          LLAMA_SERVER_BIN for a supervised llama.cpp server, or rely on cloud keys.
          The model picker shows which engines are actually up.

- Back up the state: snapshot the SQLite database file (and uploaded
          documents, where stored alongside it) on a schedule; that single file is the whole
          workspace.

Environment variable names listed here (AUTH_SECRET, INVITE_CODE,
        REGISTRATION_MODE, LLAMA_SERVER_BIN, and the provider keys) are
        the ones documented on this page; consult the repository’s example environment file
        for the complete, current list.

## Limitations and Future Work

- Single-node by design: one app process, one SQLite file, one writer at a time. There is no horizontal scaling story; the design optimizes for a self-hoster or a small team, not a fleet.

- Local quality ceiling: local models are bounded by the host’s RAM and VRAM. The fit tagging prevents crashes, but it cannot make a small model answer like a frontier one; cloud providers remain the escape hatch.

- Tool trust: web search and document chat ingest untrusted text, and prompt-injection hardening is a design goal rather than a proven control (see AI Security).

- Streaming resilience: long streamed answers can still drop on flaky networks; reconnection handling exists, but treating every stream as resumable is ongoing work.

- Unaudited security surface: rate limiting, audit logging, and at-rest secret encryption are not yet documented as implemented.

Future work builds on the roadmap above: deeper document intelligence with cited answers,
        voice input and output, a plugin system so integrations do not require forking, and
        continued mobile UI refinement for the installable PWA.

## References

- Next.js documentation, the application framework and API routes.

- Ollama, local model runtime and model library.

- llama.cpp, the inference engine behind the supervised local server.

- SQLite documentation, the embedded database that stores the workspace.

- better-sqlite3, the Node.js SQLite binding used by the data layer.

- Auth.js, the authentication library behind accounts and sessions.

- Chakor repository and project documentation.

**Q: Citation formats**

# Homelab Server Room

# Homelab Server Room

Written by [Taki Sadik](../../about.html) · Last updated 2026-10-22 · 7 min read

The cozy basement room where the entire self-hosted stack physically lives: racked hardware, managed switching, and the cable plant behind the 7-node cluster

## Overview

In one sentence: this project is the physical layer of everything else on this
        site, a dedicated basement server room that houses the hardware, switching, power, and cable
        plant behind the Proxmox hosts, the 7-node Kubernetes cluster, and the nine self-hosted services.

Software pages describe what runs; this page describes where it runs. The room holds
        3 desktop PCs and 4 laptops acting as bare-metal
        Proxmox VE 8.x hosts, a managed switch with 802.1Q VLAN
        trunking, a router handling inter-VLAN routing, DHCP, and NAT, and a
        5 GHz wireless radio in bridge mode that extends the cluster network to the
        laptop nodes. Every logical design on this site, the VLAN segmentation, the storage network,
        the zero-trust access layer, ultimately terminates in a physical port, cable, or radio link
        in this room.

The engineering problem a server room solves is not compute, it is order: one known
        place for every device, one known path for every cable, one known breaker for every power
        feed, and one known procedure when something fails at 2 AM. Status: active and in
        daily use; this is the verified physical environment behind the other infrastructure
        projects, not a render or a plan.

## Requirements and Engineering Objectives

- Functional: house 7 physical hosts plus network gear with every device reachable for hands-on maintenance; provide wired Ethernet to the desktop nodes and a dedicated wireless bridge for the laptops.

- Reliability: survive single-device failure without taking down the whole lab; keep the control plane and storage nodes on the most stable wired power and network paths.

- Thermal and noise: a basement room gives passive cooling headroom and acoustic isolation from living space; no dedicated HVAC is installed, so load is kept within what ambient basement temperatures can absorb.

- Safety: power draw distributed across standard household circuits; no overloaded power bars; cable runs kept off the floor where people walk.

- Budget constraint: consumer and repurposed hardware only; no rented rack space, no cloud spend.

Measured acceptance criteria (verified against the running lab): all 7 hosts boot to Proxmox and join their clusters; wired nodes hold stable link at negotiated speed; the wireless backhaul keeps laptop nodes in Ready state after the tuning documented on the [Kubernetes page](kubernetes-infrastructure.html).

## Physical Architecture

The room is organized so that signal flow matches physical layout: uplink enters at the
        router, switching happens at the managed switch, wired hosts patch straight into the switch,
        and the wireless radio hangs off a switch trunk port to serve the laptop shelf. Power and
        data are dressed separately to keep interference and trip hazards down.

This is the physical view of the same design drawn logically on the
        [Kubernetes Infrastructure page](kubernetes-infrastructure.html). Where that page
        shows VMs, pods, and networks, this one shows racks, ports, and cables.

## Component Reference

| Component | Responsibility | Technology | Depends on | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Desktop rack (3 PCs) | Primary compute and storage; hosts the control-plane VM and Longhorn storage nodes | Proxmox VE 8.x on bare metal | Switch ports, wired power | Verified, in daily use |
| Laptop shelf (4 laptops) | Lightweight worker nodes; redundancy for non-critical workloads | Proxmox VE 8.x; Wi-Fi power saving disabled | 5 GHz bridge, chargers | Verified, in daily use |
| Managed switch | VLAN segmentation (10/20/30), trunking to router and radio | 802.1Q managed switch | Router uplink | Verified |
| Router | NAT, DHCP reservations, inter-VLAN routing, firewall rules between segments | Documented on the Kubernetes page | ISP uplink | Verified |
| 5 GHz radio | Wireless backhaul bridging laptop nodes into VLAN 20 | Bridge mode, fixed channel | Switch trunk port | Verified |
| Ops desk | Monitoring dashboards, logs, hands-on maintenance | Grafana on VLAN 10 management | Switch, management VLAN | Verified |
| Cable plant | Cat6 runs from switch to wired hosts; dressed and labeled | Cat6, hook-and-loop ties | Physical layout | Verified |
| Exact UPS model, rack brand, wattage draw | Power protection and load numbers | - | - | Unknown, not yet measured or documented |

## Power, Cooling, and Noise

Power: hosts are distributed across standard household outlets with
        daisy-chaining of power bars avoided. Exact wattage per node has not been instrumented yet;
        adding inline power metering is on the roadmap below.

Cooling: the basement location does the heavy lifting: ambient temperatures
        stay low year-round in a Canadian basement, which is also why this room doubles as the
        cold-end reference point for the [cold-soak
        battery rig](../defence/cold-soak-battery-rig.html) work. No dedicated HVAC; racks are spaced for front-to-back airflow and
        nothing is stacked exhaust-to-intake.

Noise: fan noise is contained by the room itself. Laptop nodes run cool and
        quiet; the desktops are the loudest component under sustained load, which matters mostly
        during long compile or replication jobs.

## Build Process

### Room selection and layout

Chose the basement room for ambient cooling and noise isolation. Planned the layout so the network shelf sits between the desktop rack and the laptop shelf, keeping every cable run short and the ops desk within sight of the gear.

### Power and safety

Mapped which outlets share circuits, spread the hosts across them, and kept power bars off the floor. Verified: no warm plugs or cables under sustained load, checked by hand after the first full-power evening.

### Network core

Mounted the router, switch, and radio on the network shelf. Configured the three VLANs and trunk ports exactly as documented in the [Kubernetes build](kubernetes-infrastructure.html), then patched the desktop rack to access ports on VLAN 20.

### Wireless backhaul

Fixed the 5 GHz radio to a clear channel in bridge mode and validated throughput and stability before trusting it with cluster traffic. The flapping behavior discovered here, and its fix, are documented under Challenges on the Kubernetes page.

### Cable management and labeling

Dressed data and power separately with hook-and-loop ties, labeled both ends of every run, and photographed the finished rack for the record (the hero photo above).

## Challenges and Lessons Learned

- Wireless nodes flapping: the laptop workers initially dropped heartbeats over the bridge. Fixed with a fixed channel, disabled NIC power saving, and tuned Kubernetes node timeouts. Lesson: treat a wireless link as a first-class network segment with its own failure modes, not as transparent Ethernet.

- Cable entropy: the first build had unlabeled cables; one accidental unplug cost an evening. Lesson: label both ends at install time, every time, and photograph the rack after changes.

- Thermal assumptions: one shelf position ran warmer than the rest because exhaust air recirculated. Lesson: check each shelf position by touch and sensor after loading the rack, not just the room average.

- Power distribution: with everything on one circuit the breaker margin was uncomfortable. Lesson: map circuits before racking, not after.

## Limitations and Future Work

- No UPS is documented yet; a utility outage stops the lab. Prioritized: add UPS units for the network shelf and desktop rack, with NUT (Network UPS Tools) reporting into Prometheus.

- Power draw per node is unmeasured. Planned: inline smart plugs with power monitoring feeding Grafana.

- No environmental sensors in the room. Planned: a temperature and humidity sensor on the monitoring VLAN with alert thresholds.

- The wireless backhaul is a single point of failure for the laptop nodes. Acceptable for a homelab; documented rather than hidden.

- This page documents the photographed lab only. The larger stated estate (24-unit OptiPlex hosting fleet, 4 JBOD enclosures, the separate GPU rental stack, and the Raspberry Pi utility server) is tracked asset-by-asset with verification statuses in the Infrastructure Asset Register.

## Related Work

- Infrastructure Asset Register, the full physical and logical inventory with verification statuses, including the stated expansion hardware and the GPU-cluster feasibility analysis.

- Kubernetes Infrastructure, the 7-node cluster whose physical hosts live in this room.

- Proxmox Zero-Trust Private Cloud, the access layer for the services racked here.

- Proxmox Homelab, the single-host virtualization build that preceded the rack.

- Self-Hosted DNS, one of the services running on this hardware.

# Infrastructure Asset Register

# Infrastructure Asset Register

The physical and logical inventory behind the TYFSADIK homelab: what is confirmed running, what is stated but not yet evidenced, and what is planned, with every claim labeled by verification status.

## How to Read This Register

In one sentence: this page is the single source of truth for what hardware
        and logical infrastructure exists behind this portfolio, what state each asset is in, and
        what evidence backs each claim.

Every asset carries one of four verification statuses. They mean specific things and are
        never blurred:

- CONFIRMED: direct evidence exists on this site or in the lab itself: a photograph, a configuration that is applied and running, or output captured from the live system. The server room page is the photographic record for the confirmed rows.

- PARTIALLY VERIFIED: the asset has been stated by the owner (the person who runs this site) but independent corroborating evidence has not yet been published: no photo, no captured inventory output, no serial-level record. Treat the quantity and model as accurate to the owner's account, pending the evidence items in the verification checklist below.

- PLANNED: an intended future capability. Designed and scoped, not purchased or deployed. Nothing in a PLANNED row should be read as operational.

- UNKNOWN: insufficient evidence to record a value at all. The field is left marked rather than filled with a guess.

Two rules follow from the site's documentation philosophy (evidence first, explanation
        second, presentation third). First, this register never converts an owner statement into a
        confirmed fact; status changes only when evidence lands. Second, physical assets, virtual
        machines, containers, and logical services are kept in separate inventories: a
        Kubernetes node is a VM on a Proxmox host, not a physical server, and counting it as one
        would double-count the fleet.

Register last reconciled: 2026-10-21. Evidence source for all
        non-CONFIRMED rows: owner statement, 2026-10-21 (updated the same day with
        configuration-level testimony for the GPU stack nodes and the estate's build sequence),
        unless a row says otherwise.

        Expansion rows describe the stated next phase of the build. Specifications are recorded
